title: Five American Narrative Poems Every Parent Should Read to Their Children
author: Restoring the West
summary: Restoring the West argues that narrative poetry, once a core part of every American child's education until World War II, should be restored to family reading routines because it pairs beautiful language with memorable stories that shape moral imagination. Drawing on Catherine Dobson's research on the benefits of memorized poetry for public speaking, writing, and cultural transmission, the piece explains why classrooms largely abandoned narrative verse once modern poets turned to free verse and abstraction. It recommends five classic narrative poems for parents to read aloud, from "A Visit from St. Nicholas" to "The Village Blacksmith," each chosen for its memorability and moral or cultural content. The piece concludes that while children outgrow nursery rhymes, they need not outgrow poetry altogether, and urges parents to make verse part of bedtime routines.
points: Argues narrative poetry's disappearance from classrooms after WWII broke a centuries-old chain of cultural and moral transmission.
Cites Catherine Dobson's research that memorizing poetry builds public-speaking and writing skill alongside moral instruction.
Recommends five specific poems spanning patriotism, labor, wonder, and childhood as a bridge beyond Mother Goose.
Frames poetry reading as a parental responsibility carried out at bedtime, not solely a school subject.
quotes: In her 2012 book, Heart Beats: Everyday Life and the Memorized Poem, Catherine Dobson recounts how memorizing poetry can improve public speaking and writing, impart moral instruction, and transmit culture.
Until World War II, narrative poetry was part of every child's education. But as modern poets abandoned rhyme and story for abstraction and free verse, classrooms followed.
This short poem tells of the daily life, joys, and sorrows of an unnamed blacksmith in a small town. It celebrates the hard work, responsibility, family, and faith at the heart of everyday life.

Children may outgrow Mother Goose, but they should not outgrow beautiful poetry. Narrative poems pair rich language with simple, memorable stories that stay with young children, opening a path to a lifelong love of poetry.
